issues.legal_issue: A settlement and repayment of a debt do not justify quashing a criminal prosecution where the allegations disclose serious banking fraud involving forged documents and fictitious entities with consequences beyond a private dispute.
material_facts: The chargesheet alleged that borrowers concealed and misstated existing liabilities to obtain credit facilities from a public bank, then diverted working-capital funds contrary to the stated purpose and deprived the bank of security.
The chargesheet further alleged that letters of credit were obtained for fictitious companies and discounted using bogus bills, with some proceeds used for personal benefit.
During the prosecution, the bank’s debt was settled, a no-due certificate was issued, and a guarantor’s liability was discharged.
The High Court quashed the prosecution on the basis of settlement and the no-due certificate without addressing the allegations of fictitious companies and forged bills.
The Supreme Court held that the alleged conduct was not merely a private or predominantly civil wrong, but implicated collective and societal financial interests.
issues.conclusion: The settlement and no-due certificate did not justify quashing the prosecution. The High Court’s order was set aside and the trial was directed to proceed in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction reflected also in Article 226 of the Constitution, quashing must serve the ends of justice or prevent abuse of process. Gian Singh v. State of Punjab permits quashing after settlement in suitable cases with a predominantly civil character, but requires due regard to the nature and gravity of the offence and excludes serious offences affecting society. Narinder Singh v. State of Punjab applies those considerations, including whether conviction is remote and bleak and continuation would cause oppression or injustice. CBI v. Jagjit Singh recognizes the harmful public effect of banking offences involving dishonest inducement and forged documents. Gopakumar B. Nair v. CBI distinguishes cases involving more serious charges from cases involving only conspiracy and cheating; Narendra Lal Jain v. CBI and Nikhil Merchant v. CBI concerned materially different circumstances. The court must examine the full allegations and the substance of the settlement; repayment alone does not convert alleged financial fraud with a serious societal impact into a private civil dispute.

rule.if: criminal_quashing_appeal and settlement_based_quashing_request and public_bank_fraud_alleged and forged_trade_documents_alleged and fictitious_beneficiaries_alleged and repayment_or_no_due_certificate_issued and allegations_have_societal_financial_impact

predicates.criminal_quashing_appeal: A party brings a criminal appeal challenging an order that quashed a prosecution.
predicates.settlement_based_quashing_request: The accused seeks to end the prosecution on the basis that the dispute with the affected lender has been settled.
predicates.public_bank_fraud_alleged: The prosecution alleges dishonest conduct in obtaining or using funds from a public bank.
predicates.forged_trade_documents_alleged: The prosecution alleges that forged or bogus commercial documents were used in the alleged scheme.
predicates.fictitious_beneficiaries_alleged: The prosecution alleges that credit instruments benefited companies that were fictitious or lacked genuine commercial activity.
predicates.repayment_or_no_due_certificate_issued: The accused or borrower settled the debt and the lender issued confirmation that nothing remained due.
predicates.allegations_have_societal_financial_impa: The alleged conduct affects collective financial interests and is not confined to a private dispute between the accused and lender.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges settlement-based quashing of a prosecution alleging public-bank fraud through forged documents and fictitious beneficiaries with societal financial impact, repayment or a no-due certificate does not prevent the prosecution from continuing.
